title: Coffin Ships: How British Shipowners Monetized Drowned Crews Until One MP Drew the Line

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Shipowners pocketed freight revenue from vessels loaded past any safe draught, knowing that over-insured hulls would pay out on loss — the freight skim was underwritten by the coffins the crews sailed in.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The law of the sea put no load-line duty on owners: freeboard was a matter of contract and custom, and the marine insurance market priced the practice in rather than refusing it, structurally normalizing the coffin-ship economy.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Casualty statistics were scattered across registries and Lloyd's listings, and wreck inquests were local and brief; the systematic pattern — overloaded, over-insured, lost with all hands — was invisible until Plimsoll assembled it in Parliament.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was the freight-and-payout duality: owners whose ships sank often collected more than owners whose ships arrived, making mass death a rational business model sustained by the insurance market's pricing.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The shipowners' bloc in Parliament fought every load-line bill to a compromise, and the Merchant Shipping (Load Line) Act 1876 passed only softened — owner-empowered enforcement, diluted penalties, and Plimsoll briefly suspended from the Commons for refusing to accept the watering-down.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Plimsoll's campaign inherited the Victorian liberal-reform machinery of Royal Commissions and Commons select committees, and ran it against an owners' interest seated in both Houses.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The 1876 Act created the load-line obligation itself — the state marking on every hull of the maximum safe draught — a permanent, visible, inspection-based safety framework where none had existed.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The diluted enforcement left owners collecting on pre-load-line losses while the new marking re-valued survivors' freight rates upward; the industry absorbed the reform as a cost, not a forfeiture, with no liability reopened for the drowned.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: The load line became universal standard practice in merchant shipping, and the pattern — a safety marking fought to a compromised first law — stands behind every later maritime safety regime, including the SOLAS convention after the Titanic.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: The cozy Victorian image of Plimsoll the saintly MP versus a few wicked greedy owners — a morality tale with one hero and some villains.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The decoy personalizes a structural machine: the profits flowed from the insurance market's pricing of loss, from Parliamentary representation of the owning class, and from the absence of any marking duty at all — not from a handful of rogue characters.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The ledger is the coffin-ship economics: overload, heavy overinsurance, payout on sinking, and a legislative fight recorded in Hansard against owners who profited when crews drowned; the 1876 Merchant Shipping (Load Line) Act and its load line are the surviving framework, and Plimsoll's Commons suspension for disorderly protest is on the record.
